# KilnOps talk track

> Independent analysis using public information and synthetic data. Not affiliated with or endorsed by Varaha.

## 90-second walkthrough

> "Varaha has publicly said its Agnisparsh project plans about 450 Kon-Tiki kilns and more than 100,000 tonnes in 2027. I wanted to know what has to be true for that to work, so I built the control tower an ops team would use to run it, on synthetic data.
>
> **First, the arithmetic.** 100,000 over 450 kilns is about 222 net tonnes per kiln-year, roughly 263 once you allow for the ramp. On published Kon-Tiki performance, a typical kiln gets nowhere near that: the network would deliver about 44.1k tonnes. So the plan has to rest on a design point I can name: 2.5-tonne batches in about 3-cubic-metre kilns, 1.8 batches a day, and feedstock dried below 15% moisture, which cuts the methane deduction from 41% to 7% of gross removals.
>
> **Second, uncertainty.** That design point gives 103.7k tonnes if everything is nominal. Across 5,000 Monte Carlo runs the P50 is 68.4k, because most inputs sit at the good end of their range. The plan needs about 32k tonnes of contingency.
>
> **Third, where to buy it.** The lever simulator ranks options by rupees per incremental tonne. Fixing dMRV evidence capture recovers tonnes at about ₹1,336 a tonne. Every capacity lever costs about ₹9,728, close to full unit cost. So fix MRV before adding kilns.
>
> **Finally, integrity.** In the farmer ledger, one site paid villages late. Four to six weeks later its supply roughly halved. Paying farmers on time is a delivery control, and it is also what buyers and rating agencies check.
>
> The output is a one-page COO memo with five Q1 actions, each with an owner, a metric and a date, plus a site-launch SOP."

## Likely questions

**1. Why is your persistence factor 0.80?**
It's the IPCC 2019 Refinement default for medium-temperature pyrolysis. Kon-Tiki's main zone reaches 680–750 °C (Schmidt 2016), which would justify the high-temperature value of 0.89. I stayed conservative because distributed kilns have mixed temperature histories and Indian soils are warm, which shortens persistence in decay models. It is methodology-dependent, so it's the first thing I'd confirm with the carbon team. Moving to 0.89 adds about 12% to net tonnes.

**2. What would you measure first on day 1?**
Dry feedstock per batch and batches per running kiln-day, from batch logs at 3–5 sites. They are the two longest amber bars in the tornado, and they separate the 44.1k-tonne world from the 100k-tonne world. The scales and timestamps the dMRV system already captures give both, so it costs almost nothing.

**3. How would you cut ₹/t by 15%?**
Feedstock is 69% of cost, so the lever is tonnes of CO₂ per kilogram of residue, not the residue price. Three moves: lift the pass rate about 5 pp (the same residue earns more credits), keep moisture at or below 15% (the CH₄ deduction falls from 20% to 7% of gross if drying is slipping), and confirm high-temperature persistence if the methodology allows it. Each spreads the same biomass spend over more tonnes. Cutting the biomass price would erode supply, as the ledger shows.

**4. Your P50 is below the target. Are you saying 100k is unrealistic?**
No. I'm saying the plan has a design point that works, and every input is set at its nominal value. The P50 tells you how much buffer to build: about 32k tonnes. The lever list prices that buffer, and the top three levers close 94% of it. The real data might also put throughput higher than my ranges, which would close the gap on its own.

**5. Why trust synthetic data?**
I don't trust it for levels. I use it to prove the control tower would catch the things that matter: the new-operator evidence spike, MRV-weak sites and the payment-to-supply lag. Every generator parameter is in the yaml and tagged as a synthetic-data design choice. Swap in real parquet files with the same schema and every page runs on them.

**6. What is the biggest risk you haven't modelled?**
Correlated downside. My Monte Carlo draws inputs independently, but a bad monsoon hits residue supply, moisture and operating days together. A correlated run would widen the P10. The second is credit price: at $90 every tonne loses money, so price risk is as big as delivery risk.

**7. Why does a dMRV QA desk beat adding kilns?**
A rejected batch has already paid for residue, labour and water. Recovering it only costs evidence review, about ₹1,336 a tonne. A new tonne from a new kiln carries the full variable cost, about ₹9,728 a tonne. Rejections cost 14.4k tonnes in the synthetic year, and the top two reasons (missing temperature log, missing / unusable photos) are 44% of them. Both are hardware-and-checklist problems.

**8. How would this work in Côte d'Ivoire?**
The playbook has an annex, flagged as hypotheses. The feedstock changes (cocoa pod husk, cashew shells), payments move to mobile money, training goes into French and local languages, and the monsoon calendar becomes two rainy seasons. The control tower stays the same: the same KPIs with new thresholds.

## Resume bullet

> Built **KilnOps**, a delivery control tower for a 450-kiln distributed biochar network (Python, Streamlit, LaTeX). It covers a closed-form "what has to be true" solver, a 5,000-run Monte Carlo (P50 68.4k t vs a 100k target) and a lever simulator showing dMRV fixes recover tonnes at ₹1,336/t, 7× cheaper than new capacity. It also includes 14 KPIs on 218 sourced assumptions, a COO memo and a site-launch SOP.
